title: Trent: meritorious cause is Christ's passion alone
source_text: XXXVIII. Atque hac etiam in parte, consentientes habemus ipsos Pontificios. Nam totam hominis impii & peccatoris justificationem, quae juxta eos constat peccatorum remissione, & renovatione interioris hominis, gratuitam esse agnoscunt. Nec statuunt ullam ejus causam meritoriam praeter Christi mortem & obedientiam, ut videre est in ipso Concilio Tridentino. Nam Sess. 6. cap. 7. enumerans causas justificationis, non aliam ejus causam meritoriam recenset quam passionem Christi. Hujus, inquit, justificationis causae sunt finalis quidem gloria Dei & Christi, & vita aeterna. Efficiens vero misericors Deus, qui gratuito abluit: meritoria dilectissimus unigenitus suus Do-minus noster Jesus Christus, qui cum essemus inimici, propter nimiam charitatem, qua dilexit nos, sua sanctissima passione in ligno crucis justificationem meruit, & pro nobis Deo patri satisfecit. Capite vero sequenti, expresse negat quicquam eorum quae justificationem praecedunt, ipsam justificationis gratiam promereri. Gratis autem, in-quit, justificari ideo dicimur, quia nihil eorum quae justificationem praecedunt, sive fides, sive opera, ipsam justificationis gratiam promeretur. Si enim gratia est, jam non ex operibus; alioquin, ut Apostolus inquit, gratia jam non est gratia.
pass_a_gloss: And in this part also we have the Papists themselves agreeing. For they acknowledge that the whole justification of an ungodly and sinful man, which according to them consists in the remission of sins and the renovation of the inner man, is free. Nor do they establish any meritorious cause of it besides Christ's death and obedience, as may be seen in the Council of Trent itself. For Session 6, chapter 7, enumerating the causes of justification, recounts no other meritorious cause of it than Christ's passion. Of this justification, it says, the final cause is indeed the glory of God and of Christ, and eternal life. But the efficient cause is merciful God, who freely washes: the meritorious is his most beloved only-begotten, our Lord Jesus Christ, who when we were enemies, because of the great charity with which he loved us, by his most holy passion on the wood of the cross merited justification and satisfied God the Father for us. And in the following chapter it expressly denies that anything of those things which precede justification merits the grace of justification itself. Therefore we are said to be justified freely, it says, because nothing of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification itself. For if it is grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise, as the Apostle says, grace is no longer grace.
pass_b_english: Romans agree first justification is free; Trent's sole meritorious cause is Christ's passion.
Nothing preceding justification—faith or works—merits the grace of justification.
